In the opinion of the feathered creature who authors this page in each issue of the
D1.A.MOND, there is much to be thankful for on the part of all of us who are bound to
gether by a "chain whose diamond clasp gleams bright above each heart." To count all
our blessings would be never-ending.
Yet a few are deserving of special mention. The student uprising in the late 1960's
against all established institutions, including the fraternity system, was met by Psi
Upsilon at least as effectively as by other fraternities. We emerged in overall good
condition, our casualties few and far between.
Today, in the latter 1970's, new life has been breathed into the entire fraternity sys
tem. This is dramatically true in the Chapters of our own Fratemity. Memberships are
growing, and our Chapters are attracting some of the ablest young men on their re
spective campuses. Clearly evident is a renewed spirit of believing in and working for
the common objectives laid down by our founders. For all this we can be profoundh'
thankful. There is a tomorrow, after all, which some thought might never come.
In addition, our alumni are stirring more actively. One has only to read of the re
markable gains made in the Annual Giving returns of late to realize that more and
more of our brothers are responding to what they are witnessing in their ovwi Chapters.
There is every reason to believe that this response wUl continue to escalate, as others
become assured that Psi Upsilon as a whole, and their Chapters in particular, are
moving foi-ward to newer and higher levels.
Further, all this progress has been accomplished at a time when our country has been
experiencing runaway inflation and mounting unemployment. It speaks well for the
tenets of our brotherhood that its members can rally during this critical period, that our
Chapters can rise again and prosper, and that the work of the Executive Council is
winning ever-widening support.
Now we leam that the Delta Chapter at New York University has been selected to
host the 134th Convention this coming summer. Some may have forgotten that the
Delta was Psi Upsilon's second Chapter established, its first expansion Chapter. It also
should be remembered that the Delta hosted the first Convention of our Fraternity in
1841, the first Convention of any fratemity.
The Delta, as it happens, is in New York City! Despite all the trials and tribulations
of that beleaguered metropolis, there are those who stUl believe it to be the center, the
core, of our business world, our culture, our entertainment, and all that makes up the
fabric of our American way of life. The magnet which is New York should attract an
unusually large number of brothers to this Convention. It is a rare chance to come to
New York and to enjoy all that the Big Apple has to offer. Someone once wrote, "In
New York, just ask for it, and either you can have it or you can get it."
Owlie has made his decision�
he wUl attend the 134th Convention. And he hopes
many others will make the same decision. It would provide a great chance to join with
old friends in the spirit we knew when we joined this fine old Fratemity. It would
demonstrate to the Executive CouncU the brothers' respect and appreciation for its
continuing efforts. It would show the educational world that Psi UpsUon lives and can
be a vital asset on any campus selected for a Chapter. More than anything else, it can
be a time of renewal.
Yes, we have much to be thankful for. Here is one more opportunity to enjoy being
a part of that "chain whose diamond clasp gleams bright above each heart." See you
in August.

Albert Charles Jacobs, Phi '21 Passes on:
(1) Scholar, Teacher, Administrator
(2) Mr. Psi Upsilon

( 1 ) Psi Upsilon suffered a great loss with the pass
ing of Albert Charles Jacobs, Phi '21 on October 29,
1976. Seventy-six years of age, he died at St. Joseph
Mercy Hospital in his home town of Ann Arbor, Mich
igan.
Brother Jacobs was known to the world at large as
a brilliant legal scholar, an eminent teacher, the trust
ed right arm of General Dwdght David Eisenhower
during the latter's presidency of Columbia University,
and a distinguished president himself of two leading
institutions of higher learning.
The son of Albert Poole Jacobs, Phi '73, he was born
in Birmingham, Michigan and attended pubhc schools
in Birmingham and Ann Arbor before entering the
University of Michigan. Though his studies there were
interrupted by World War I, during which he served
as an Army private, he returned to earn a baccalau
reate degree with his class as a Phi Beta Kappa
scholar "with high distinction."
Selected upon graduation as one of the nation's
Rhodes Scholars, a coveted honor, he entered Oxford
University in the fall of 1921, enrolhng at Oriel Col
lege. There he received "First Class Honors" in juris
prudence after three years, as well as degrees of Bach
elor of Civil Law and Master of Arts. Only iiiose close
to him know that a temporary eye afflction prevented
him from pursuing his studies for the entire last term
and led him to settle in a small EngHsh seacoast town
during this period before sitting for his degree exam
inations.
For three additional years Brother Jacobs remained
at Oxford, teaching law as a lecturer and fellow at
Oriel College and a lecturer at Braenose. In so doing
he attained the further distinction of becoming the
first American to serve as a fulltime fellow, or don, at
Oxford.
Upon his retum to the United States in 1927, Dr.
Jacobs joined the Columbia Law School faculty and
quickly rose to a full professorship. He authored sev
eral books on domestic and family relations law dur
ing this period, his case books on domestic relations
and on tenant-landlord relations becoming standard
texts.
His campus life was interrupted a second time by
the outbreak of World War II. As a captain in the
Navy he was assigned to Washington as director of
the Navy's casualties and dependents welfare division.
He was awarded the Legion of Merit for his eflForts
in revising the Navy's casualty administration pro
cedures and for his responsibilities for the service
men's dependence allowance act and the missing per
sons act.
In 1946 Brother Jacobs retumed to Columbia Uni
versity as assistant to the president in charge of
veterans' affairs. He later noted that teaching always
remained his first love and that he had resisted insofar
as possible this and subsequent appointments to ad
ministrative positions.
General Eisenhower became president of Columbia
the following year and named him provost. The an
nouncement of the appointment stated that Dr.
Jacobs would be Eisenhower's "principal assistant"
and act as "alter ego and successor" during the presi
dent's frequent absences. For the next two years the
provost often served as spokesman for the University.
Now Brother Jacobs' time increasingly was con
sumed by administrative chores, and his busy sched
ule held his family in New York City ahnost the year
round. It was their pressure that led him to accept the
post of chancellor at the University of Denver in
1949, where he doubled as professor of law. Here he
insisted that scholarship take precedence over athlet
ics and accordingly siphoned money from the alumni
fund to increase faculty salaries. In a sweeping re-

Brother Jacobs' interests spread far beyond aca

Church Executive Council and was honored by being
elected a lay deputy to two of the Triennial Generd
Conventions of the Episcopal Church. In 1962 he
helped form the Foundation of Episcopal Colleges,
becoming its first chairman.
Active in the RepubHcan party. Brother Jacobs was
a 1959 member of the RepubHcan National Com
mittee on Program and Progress, as weU as chairman
of its Task Force on National Security and Peace. He
was an alternate delegate from Connecticut to the
RepubHcan National Convention in 1960. Two years
earHer he served as chairman of the United States
Delegation to the 41st (Maritime) Session of the In
ternational Labour Organization in Geneva, Switzer
land. He retumed from this assignment talking of a
firsthand view of Communist poHtical tactics.
Upon his retirement from Trinity as president emer
itus, he and Mrs. Jacobs moved back to Ann Arbor
and also maintained a summer home on Chappaquiddick Island, Edgartovra, Massachusetts. At that time
he became chairman of the Board of Directors of tiie
Federal Home Loan Bank of Boston, having served
several years as pubHc interest director. Other re
sponsibilities included directorships of the Connecti
cut General Life Insurance Company, the Aetna In
surance Company, and the Institute of Living in Hart
ford.
A firm believer in the value of a strong Hberal arts
education and a proven educational leader of stature,
Dr. Jacobs received fifteen honorary degrees during
the course of his career, ten of these being Doctor of
Laws. He was always proud to note that six had been
conferred by coUeges and universities witii active
Chapters of his beloved Psi Upsilon.
He leaves his wiie, Loretta Field Beal Jacobs,
whom he married in 1927 and whose father had been
a regent of the University of Michigan for thirty-two
years; two daughters, Mrs. LeRoy Butcher of Sara
sota, Florida, and Mrs. Karl D. Malcolm, Jr. of Ann
Arbor; a son, Travis B. Jacobs, Lambda '62, of Mid
dlebury, Vermont; a sister, Mrs. Charlotte M. New
man, of Ann Arbor; and six grandchildren.
At Dr. Jacobs' funeral in Ann Arbor undergraduates
from the Phi Chapter served as pallbearers. A beau
tiful memorial service was conducted in the Trinity
CoUege Chapel on November 19, with members of
the Beta Beta Chapter as ushers.

Anniversary Celebrated at
Williamsburg

Just five months and a day after the signing of the
Declaration of Independence in 1776 the first Amer
ican society bearing a Greek letter name was founded.
It was in the Apollo Room of the Raleigh Tavern at
WilHamsburg, Virginia, the same room where Patrick
Henry deHvered his "Give me Hberty or give me
death" speech. Here five students of WilHam and Mary
College took solemn vows of friendship, moraHty, and
learning. They named their secret organization Phi
Beta Kappa.
Two hundred years later this historic event was
commemorated by a retum to Williamsburg of repre
sentatives from the forty-seven college fraternities
currentiy in the National Interfraternity Conference,
the twenty-six sororities in the National Panhellenic
Conference, the twenty-nine fratemities in the Pro
fessional Interfraternity Conference, and the fourteen
sororities in the Professional Panhellenic Conference.
The program on December 2 was divided appropri
ately into three sessions: "A Look to Our Past," "The
Present," and "An Eye to Our Future." Distinguished
speakers included the former Senator Margaret Chase
Smith and U.S. Senator John G. Tower.
In conjunction with the celebration an American
College Fraternity Bicentennial Commission was es
tabhshed several months earlier to "review the impact
and contribution to higher education made by the
coUege fraternity during the past two centuries" and
to "address the role of the college fratemity in the
year 2000 as related to American society and higher
education at that time." Starting with three provoc
ative major papers, four task forces, composed of
ninety educators and fraternity representatives in aU,
undertook broad areas of study, resulting in a compre
hensive report to be pubHshed shortly. The Com
mission was sponsored jointly by Indiana University
and the Fratemity Executives Association and ap
proved by the National Interfraternity Conference.
Psi Upsilon was represented appropriately both in
the work of the Commission and in attendance at the
commemorative celebration. Ours is the fifth oldest
of the Greek-letter fraternities wiih a continuous
record of existence. Kappa Alpha Society, Sigma Phi,
and Delta Phi, known as the "Union Triad," were
founded at Union CoUege between 1825 and 1827.
Alpha Delta Phi had its beginnings at Hamilton in
1832, one year before our Fraternity made its ap
pearance at Union. This coUege gave birth to six fra
temities in aU and is referred to by many as the
"Mother of Fratemities." Psi Upsilon often is linked
with Alpha Delta Phi and Delta Kappa Epsilon, es
tabhshed at Yale in 1844, in the so-called "Historical
Triad."
Meanwhile, agitation against secret societies in
1831 caused Phi Beta Kappa to become strictiy an
honorary organization, limiting its membership since
that time to undergraduates who achieve academic
distinction in the Hberal arts. Others weathered this
first test of survival, however, and by 1861, when the
Civil War interrupted fratemity grovi^ and expan
sion, twenty-six fratemities had been solidly launched.
As Psi Upstion approaches its sesquicentennial an
niversary in 1983, its members can look back on other
challenges to its survival, in common with aU fra
ternities. Yet we have not only survived every test;
we have emerged from each with fresh vitality and
greater strength. Conditions have changed radically,
of course, in the two centuries since that first meeting
in the Raleigh Tavem, but the college fratemity has
shown itself to be the single most enduring student
organization in the history of American higher educa
tion.
